name: Farasan Islands Marine Reserve
blurb: Seagrass, dugongs and gazelles on coral islands in the southern Red Sea.

tip.title: Lose the seagrass
tip.text: Dugongs and green turtles graze seagrass. Set Seagrass to -100% and watch them, then the orcas that hunt young dugongs.

notes: The species list comes from GBIF occurrence records inside a circle around the park, so it can include nearby areas. Feeding links come from GloBI records and the sources listed where they state them; others are general ecology and are illustrative.

nodes.name: Sunlight
nodes.desc: Strong sun in clear shallow water drives seagrass, mangroves and plankton, and warms the reef lagoons.

nodes.name: Warm shallow sea
nodes.desc: The Red Sea around the islands is warm and salty, with shallow banks where seagrass beds and coral grow.

nodes.name: Scarce rainfall
nodes.desc: Rain is scarce in this arid region, so land plants on the islands depend on the little that falls.

nodes.name: Bacteria & scavenging invertebrates
nodes.desc: Break down dead seagrass, mangrove litter and carcasses, returning nutrients to sediment and water.

nodes.name: Seagrass
nodes.desc: Underwater meadows in shallow lagoons. Seagrasses of the genus Halophila are a main food of dugongs.

nodes.name: Grey mangrove
nodes.desc: A salt-tolerant tree recorded on the islands that holds shoreline sediment and shelters young marine life.

nodes.name: Phytoplankton
nodes.desc: Microscopic drifting algae that base the open-water food chain, feeding copepods and small fish.

nodes.name: Acacia shrubs
nodes.desc: Thorny desert trees and shrubs. Wikipedia lists acacia leaves, flowers and fruit as the main food of Arabian gazelles.

nodes.name: Dugong
nodes.desc: Grazes seagrass, roots included. Wikipedia notes few natural predators, though orcas and sharks threaten young animals.

nodes.name: Green sea turtle
nodes.desc: Adults mostly graze seagrass and algae. Islands in the area host nesting sea turtles, including endangered green turtles.

nodes.name: Copepods
nodes.desc: Tiny crustaceans in the plankton that graze phytoplankton and feed schooling fish.

nodes.name: Arabian gazelle
nodes.desc: A selective browser of acacia and other woody plants. About a thousand live on the Farasan Islands.

nodes.name: Sardines
nodes.desc: Schooling plankton-feeding fish that carry energy from plankton up to seabirds, dolphins and ospreys.

nodes.name: Spinner dolphin
nodes.desc: Recorded in the waters off the islands. It hunts small fish and squid in groups.

nodes.name: Brown booby
nodes.desc: Seabird recorded often near the islands. It plunge-dives for fish.

nodes.name: Pink-backed pelican
nodes.desc: The most recorded bird near the islands. It scoops fish from shallow waters.

nodes.name: Ghost crab
nodes.desc: Sand-dwelling crabs that scavenge on beaches and take hatchling turtles, according to the turtle source.

nodes.name: Crab-plover
nodes.desc: A wading shorebird recorded on the islands that specialises in eating crabs.

nodes.name: Egyptian vulture
nodes.desc: A small scavenging vulture recorded on the islands. It feeds on carrion and scraps.

nodes.name: Osprey
nodes.desc: Fish are about 99 percent of its diet. It plunge-dives for live fish and is a well-recorded bird here.

nodes.name: Orca
nodes.desc: An occasional visitor to the islands. It hunts dolphins and can take young dugongs.
